summary:
Voyage: Exploring the Unforgotten is a browser game for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge Abandoned but not Forgotten. It turns NASA’s retired Mars rovers into a playable story for ages 10–17.

You pilot a new rover sent to find three real rovers left behind: Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity. After a narrated launch, you steer through space, dodging debris and spotting real spacecraft like Mars Odyssey and Phobos. Then you land on Mars, with a flashback to Sojourner’s 1997 airbag touchdown.

On the surface, each site recreates the real hazard its rover faced: cold, soft soil, or a planet-wide dust storm. You survive it using the lesson that rover teaches. Discovering each rover unlocks its archive in the Rover Hub:

real NASA photos
an illustrated mission story
an interactive 3D model
an AI chat that speaks in the rover’s own voice, strictly from curated NASA facts, so nothing is invented

At the end, your own rover is left behind on Mars, watching Earth as a distant dot. The one who carried their stories home becomes the next to be remembered.

Voyage is built with Phaser 3, Next.js and three.js and runs from a single shareable URL. It features pixelated 2.5D art, voice narration with subtitles, and an offline chat fallback, so it never stalls in a live demo. The gameplay is the message: bringing their stories back is exactly what the challenge asks.

details:
What it does and how it works

Voyage is a browser game, about 10 minutes long, that tells the true stories of NASA’s three retired Mars rovers: Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity. You play a fictional modern rover sent to find them.

  1. Launch: a narrated liftoff from Earth, voiced by Mission Control.
  2. Space travel: a steering mini-game where you stay inside a trajectory corridor and dodge debris. Real spacecraft drift past with short facts: a spent Delta II stage, Mars Odyssey and Phobos.
  3. Landing: a sky-crane touchdown, with a flashback to Pathfinder’s 1997 airbag landing that ends on a real NASA photo.
    • Sojourner: cold and limited solar power.
    • Spirit: soft soil, solved with traction mode.
    • Opportunity: a planet-wide dust storm, survived with power preservation.
    • real NASA photos with a fullscreen viewer
    • an illustrated mission story with planned-versus-actual lifespan bars
    • an interactive 3D model
    • an AI chat where the rover answers in the first person
    • Your rover spends its last coins on an emergency charge.
    • A gust damages its solar panels, and the battery drains to zero.
    • The rover shuts down. It can’t move or call home.
    • A “Signal lost” message notes that Opportunity went silent in a storm like this in June 2018.
    • In a quiet final scene, your powerless rover sits under the settling dust, looking at Earth as a single distant point of light. It speaks its last words: “I came all this way to remember the ones who were left behind. Maybe... someday... someone will remember me, too.”
    • The game closes on Data Beamed Home: each rover’s dates and a one-line epitaph, the stories you carried back.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Learning by doing: players don’t just read about Spirit getting stuck or Opportunity going silent; they live through it and learn why it happened.
  • Real material: NASA photos, NASA’s 3D model, and facts checked against NASA/JPL sources.
  • Low barrier: one link, no install, works on school computers.
  • Emotional connection: players go through the same kind of loss the rovers did, so the theme lands as a feeling rather than a fact. The goal is for players aged 10–17 to leave curious about planetary science, and to feel that these machines, and the people behind them, deserve to be remembered.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.
    • Next.js and React for the interface and server
    • Phaser 3 for the game
    • three.js for the 3D model viewer
    • Tailwind CSS for styling
    • Google Gemini powers the rover chat, through a server-side route.
    • ElevenLabs generated the narration voices.
    • AI image generation produced the pixel art.
    • Claude assisted with coding.
  • Audio: music and sound effects are synthesized live with the Web Audio API.
  • Asset pipeline: sharp and ffmpeg, for compressing images, 3D models and audio.
  • Hosting: Vercel, deployed from GitHub.
  • Hardware: standard laptops only.

Creativity

  • Each rover’s real hazard becomes the gameplay for its site, so the mission history is the mechanic rather than a menu of facts.
  • The AI chat lets players ask a rover questions directly, but it may only answer from that rover’s verified fact sheet. Anything else gets “I don’t remember.”
  • The ending reverses the player’s role. You spend the game rescuing forgotten rovers, then your own rover meets Opportunity’s fate. You lose power, then contact, and become the next explorer left behind. That puts the challenge theme, Abandoned but not Forgotten, in the player’s own hands.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy:
    • Every fact, date (UTC) and number comes from NASA/JPL sources.
    • The chat cannot invent answers, and it falls back to a scripted offline answer if the connection fails.
    • The API key stays on the server.
    • The chat is rate-limited and refuses off-topic or rule-breaking requests.
    • Subtitles are always on, so the game works with the sound off.
    • It is fully playable by keyboard and respects reduced-motion settings.
    • The text is written for younger readers.
  • Reliability: an offline chat fallback and compressed assets keep live demos smooth.
    • NASA images and models are labelled and credited, and AI-generated content is acknowledged in the credits.
    • The game uses no NASA logos and implies no NASA endorsement.
